lessons.title: Inside the Rack — The Physical Anatomy of a Colo Server

children.text: A colocation contract is a legal agreement. What actually lands inside NSE's data centre is a physical box: a server, a switch, a bundle of cables, and a power connection that a firm's own engineers will not be able to walk over and fix at 3 a.m. Everything about how that rack gets built has to account for that one constraint.
What's Actually Sitting in the Rack

markDefs.definition: A network switch mounted at the top of a server rack, connecting the servers in that rack to the wider network with the shortest possible cable runs.

children.text: A typical HFT footprint inside a colocation facility is small, often a quarter rack or half rack rather than a full one. Inside it sits one or more compact trading servers, a

that connects those servers to the exchange's network and to each other, a patch panel where the firm's cross-connect cable terminates, and a power distribution unit feeding everything from the facility's mains.

body.caption: What's inside a typical HFT colo rack

cells: Runs the strategy logic and order gateway software
Connects servers in the rack to each other and to the exchange's network
Termination point for the cross-connect cable running to the exchange's core network
Distributes mains power to every device in the rack, often with two independent feeds
Stamps packets with a precise time as they arrive or leave, covered in more depth in the next chapter

stats.label: Standard Rack Height
stats.context: A U (rack unit) is about 4.45 cm. A standard full-height rack holds 42 of them.

stats.label: Typical HFT Footprint
stats.context: Most colocated HFT setups use far less than a full rack, since the workload is compute-light but latency-critical

stats.label: Cross-connect Length
stats.context: Kept as short as physically possible, since every extra metre of fibre adds a small, fixed amount of propagation delay

children.text: High-density racks draw more power and produce more heat per square metre than a typical office server room, which is one reason colocation facilities are purpose-built data centres rather than repurposed office space. Firms then choose how much redundancy to pay for on top of that baseline.

columns.label: Non-redundant
points: Single power feed and single network path into the rack
A single power or network fault can take the entire strategy offline

columns.label: Redundant
points: Dual power feeds from independent sources, often backed by the facility's own UPS and generators
A single fault degrades performance instead of causing a full outage

body.text: A colocation contract does not automatically include redundant power and network paths. Firms choose, and pay for, how much single-point-of-failure risk they are willing to accept, and it is a decision made once, at setup, not something adjusted mid-trading-day.

children.text: You Can't Just Walk In: Access and Remote Hands

markDefs.definition: A service offered by data centre and exchange colocation operators where on-site staff perform basic physical tasks, like rebooting a server or replacing a cable, on a client firm's behalf, since the client's own engineers typically cannot access the facility directly.

children.text: Exchange data centres are highly restricted environments, typically requiring biometric access, escorted entry, and logged visits for anyone stepping near the racks. A firm's own engineers usually cannot simply walk in to fix a server. Instead, most colocation contracts include, or allow a firm to purchase,
: on-site facility staff who can power-cycle a server, re-seat a cable, or swap a failed component on the firm's instructions, without the firm's own staff ever entering the building.

body.title: Before You Ship a Server to the Colo
steps: Asset-tag and document every server and cable, since your own engineers may never physically see the rack again after installation.
Confirm whether the contract includes redundant power and network paths, or whether that is a separate, chargeable upgrade.
Install and verify any hardware timestamping card before shipment, since accessing it later means a remote hands request.
Pre-configure remote monitoring and alerting, so a fault is caught before it becomes a call to the facility's remote hands desk.
Write a short runbook that a non-engineer remote hands technician could follow over the phone during an outage.

body.label: Access Control
body.context: Standard practice at exchange colocation facilities, reflecting their status as systemically important market infrastructure.

body.text: A colocation rack is not a server you own. It is a server you can only touch through someone else's hands, so everything about how you build and monitor it has to assume you will never be in the room.

points: A typical HFT colocation footprint is small, often a quarter or half rack, containing a trading server, a top-of-rack switch, a patch panel for the cross-connect, and a power distribution unit.
Redundant power and network paths are usually a separate, chargeable choice, not an automatic feature of every colocation contract.
Exchange data centres are highly restricted, so most day-to-day physical work happens through a remote hands service rather than a firm's own staff.
Because access is so restricted, documentation, remote monitoring, and pre-shipment checks matter more here than in a typical office server room.
